content: Cochineal refers to both a crimson or carmine dye and the cochineal insect, scientifically known as Dactylopius coccus. This insect belongs to the suborder Sternorrhyncha and is the primary source of the dye. While other species within the genus Dactylopius can also produce cochineal extract, they are nearly indistinguishable from D. coccus, even for expert taxonomists. As a result, the term cochineal insect is often used generically to refer to these species. It is important to note that there is more than one species of cochineal insect. The main biological differences between these species lie in their host plant preferences and geographic distributions. D. coccus is native to tropical and subtropical regions of South America and Mexico. This insect is a sessile parasite that lives on cacti of the genus Opuntia, feeding on the moisture and nutrients within the cactus. It produces carminic acid, which serves as a defense mechanism against predation by other insects. The carminic acid can be extracted from the insect's body and eggs to create the dye. Cochineal is primarily used as a food coloring and in cosmetics. The production of natural dyes like cochineal declined after the invention of synthetic pigments and dyes, such as alizarin, in the late 19th century. However, concerns over the safety of artificial food additives have led to a resurgence in the popularity of cochineal dyes. This renewed demand has made the cultivation of cochineal insects economically viable once again. History The cochineal dye was historically used by the Aztec and Maya civilizations in Central and North America. During the 15th century, cities conquered by Montezuma paid annual tributes that included cochineal dye. During the colonial period, cochineal production expanded rapidly, particularly in Oaxaca, Mexico, where indigenous producers cultivated it. Cochineal became Mexico's second most valuable export after silver. The dye was highly prized in Europe, with its price regularly quoted on the London and Amsterdam Commodity Exchanges. After Mexico's War of Independence (1810–1821), the Mexican monopoly on cochineal ended, and large-scale production emerged in Guatemala and the Canary Islands. However, the demand for cochineal sharply declined with the advent of synthetic dyes in the mid-19th century, causing significant economic disruption in Spain. The labor-intensive process of breeding cochineal insects could not compete with modern industrial methods and lower production costs. By the 20th century, the trade in cochineal had nearly disappeared, and its cultivation was largely maintained for traditional purposes rather than commercial demand. Biology Cochineal insects are soft-bodied, flat, oval-shaped scale insects that cluster on cactus pads. They use their beak-like mouthparts to penetrate the cactus and feed on its juices, remaining immobile. After mating, fertilized females grow in size and give birth to tiny nymphs. These nymphs secrete a waxy white substance over their bodies to protect themselves from water and excessive sunlight. This waxy coating makes the insects appear white or gray externally, although their bodies produce a red pigment, giving their insides a dark purple appearance. Adult males are smaller than females and have wings. They do not feed after reaching sexual maturity and live only long enough to fertilize eggs, making them rarely observed. During the nymph stage, also known as the crawler stage, cochineal insects disperse. Juveniles move to feeding spots, produce long wax filaments, and are carried by the wind to new host cacti. Once settled, they establish feeding sites and produce a new generation. Male nymphs feed on the cactus until they mature, after which they no longer feed. Host Cacti Dactylopius coccus is native to tropical and subtropical regions of South America and Mexico, where its host cacti grow naturally. The insects have been introduced to Spain, the Canary Islands, Algeria, Australia, and Eritrea, where host cacti were either already abundant or introduced alongside the insects. There are approximately 150 species of Opuntia cacti, but the most suitable for cochineal cultivation is Opuntia ficus-indica. Feeding cochineal insects can damage or even kill their host cacti. Other species of Dactylopius also feed on many of the same Opuntia species, and the wide range of reported hosts may be due to the difficulty in distinguishing D. coccus from these less common species. Farming Cochineal farming can be done using traditional or controlled methods. In the traditional method, infected cactus pads are planted, or existing cacti are infected with cochineal insects, which are then harvested by hand. The controlled method involves placing small baskets, known as Zapotec nests, on host cacti. These baskets contain clean, fertile female insects that leave the nests, settle on the cactus, and await insemination by males. In both methods, the insects must be protected from predators, cold, and rain. The complete life cycle lasts three months, during which the cacti are kept at a constant temperature of 27°C. After the cycle, the new generation of cochineal insects can either begin the cycle again or be dried for dye production. Harvesting the insects is labor-intensive, as they must be individually knocked, brushed, or picked from the cacti and placed into bags. The insects are collected by small groups of workers who sell them to local processors or exporters. Natural enemies, including insects, birds, rodents, and reptiles, can significantly reduce cochineal populations. Effective pest control measures are essential in regions dependent on cochineal production. For small-scale cultivation, manual pest control methods are most effective and safe. For large-scale cultivation, advanced pest control methods, including bioinsecticides or pheromone traps, are necessary. Dye Production A deep crimson dye is extracted from female cochineal insects. Cochineal is used to produce scarlet, orange, and other red tints, with the coloring derived from carminic acid. The natural carminic acid content of cochineal extract is typically 19–22%. The insects are killed by immersion in hot water, exposure to sunlight, steam, or oven heat, with each method producing a different color. The insects must be dried to about 30% of their original body weight to prevent decay during storage. Approximately 155,000 insects are required to produce one kilogram of cochineal. There are two main forms of cochineal dye: cochineal extract, made from raw dried and pulverized insect bodies, and carmine, a more purified form. To prepare carmine, powdered insect bodies are boiled in an ammonia or sodium carbonate solution, filtered to remove insoluble matter, and treated with alum to precipitate the red aluminum salt of carminic acid. The absence of iron ensures color purity. Additives such as stannous chloride, citric acid, borax, or gelatin may be used to regulate the precipitate's formation. Lime can be added to produce purple shades. As of 2005, Peru produced 200 tonnes of cochineal dye annually, while the Canary Islands produced 20 tonnes. Chile and Mexico have also recently begun exporting cochineal. France is believed to be the world's largest importer, with Japan and Italy also importing significant quantities. Much of the imported cochineal is processed and re-exported to other developed economies. In 2005, the market price of cochineal ranged from 50 to 80 USD per kilogram, compared to synthetic raw food dyes priced as low as 10–20 USD per kilogram. Usage Traditionally, cochineal was used to dye fabrics. During the colonial period, its use increased with the introduction of sheep to Latin America, as it provided intense color and adhered better to wool than to pre-Hispanic materials like cotton, agave fibers, and yucca fibers. European markets quickly recognized its qualities, leading to a dramatic increase in demand. Carmine became a strong competitor to other colorants like madder root, kermes, Polish cochineal, brazilwood, and Tyrian purple, which were used to dye the clothing of royalty, nobility, and clergy. It was also used for painting, handicrafts, and tapestries. Cochineal-colored wool and cotton remain important materials for Mexican folk art and crafts. Today, cochineal is used as a fabric and cosmetics dye, a natural food coloring, and in oil paints, pigments, and watercolors. When used as a food additive, it must be labeled on packaging, sometimes as E120. Some individuals are allergic to carmine, with reactions ranging from mild hives to atrial fibrillation and anaphylactic shock. Carmine has also been linked to asthma in some cases. Cochineal is one of the colors recommended for elimination from the diets of hyperactive children by the Hyperactive Children's Support Group. Its use in food and cosmetics may render it unacceptable to strict vegetarians, as well as to many Muslims and Jews, who consider it forbidden (haram and treif) because it is derived from insects. Cochineal is one of the few water-soluble colorants resistant to degradation over time. It is highly stable against light, heat, and oxidation, surpassing many synthetic food colors in stability. The water-soluble form is used in alcoholic drinks, while the insoluble form is used in a wide variety of products. Together with ammonium carmine, it is found in meat, sausages, processed poultry products, surimi, marinades, alcoholic drinks, bakery products, cookies, desserts, icings, pie fillings, jams, preserves, gelatin desserts, juice beverages, cheddar cheese varieties, and other dairy products, sauces, and sweets. The average human consumes one to two drops of carminic acid annually through food. Carmine is considered safe for use in eye cosmetics and is widely used in the cosmetics industry for hairand skin-care products, lipsticks, face powders, rouges, and blushes. It is also used in microbiology as a bright red dye and stain. The pharmaceutical industry uses cochineal to color pills and ointments.
